rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The role of a catalyst is to change :
rows.solution: A catalyst provides an ALTERNATIVE PATH with a lower activation energy, so more molecules can clear the barrier and the reaction goes faster. It changes nothing thermodynamic: the enthalpy of reaction, the Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant are all properties of the initial and final states alone, and a catalyst changes neither state. It speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but at exactly the same position.

rows.stem: Which of the following molecules is chiral in nature ?
rows.solution: A molecule is chiral if it has a carbon carrying four different groups. In 1-chloropropane and 1-chlorobutane the carbon bearing the chlorine also carries two hydrogens. In 2-chloropropane that carbon carries two identical methyl groups. In 2-chlorobutane the second carbon carries \(-\mathrm{Cl}\), \(-\mathrm{H}\), \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) and \(-\mathrm{C_2H_5}\) — four different groups — so 2-chlorobutane is chiral.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\) can be converted to \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\) by :
rows.solution:
Converting a primary alcohol to an ALDEHYDE and stopping there needs a mild, non-aqueous oxidant. Pyridinium chlorochromate does exactly that:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{PCC}} \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)
Potassium permanganate is too strong and would carry the oxidation on to ethanoic acid. Catalytic hydrogenation and lithium aluminium hydride are REDUCING agents and would move in the wrong direction entirely.

rows.stem: The IUPAC name for \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-N(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3}\) is :
rows.solution:
Number the longest chain attached to the nitrogen: that is the three-carbon propyl group, so the parent is propan-1-amine. The other two groups on nitrogen are cited as N-substituents in alphabetical order, ethyl before methyl.
The name is N-ethyl-N-methylpropan-1-amine.

The distractors each miscount the substituents: N,N-diethyl and N,N-dimethyl both assume two identical groups, and N-methylpentan-2-amine treats the two chains as one continuous five-carbon chain through the nitrogen, which is not how amines are named.

rows.stem: A plot between concentration of reactant \([\mathrm{R}]\) and time 't' is shown below. Which of the given order of reaction is indicated by the graph ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the plot IS the question. The stem says only 'is shown below' and describes nothing about the curve, so the row is unanswerable from its text alone. Printed graph: a y-axis labelled \([\mathrm{R}]\) with \([\mathrm{R}]_0\) marked at the top, an x-axis labelled 'Time' with an arrow, an origin marked O, and a single straight line falling from \([\mathrm{R}]_0\) annotated 'k = - slope'. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
A plot of concentration against time that is a STRAIGHT LINE with a negative slope means the concentration falls at a constant rate:
\([\mathrm{R}] = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - kt\)
which is the integrated rate law for a ZERO order reaction, the slope being \(-k\). For first order the same plot would be an exponential curve, and the straight line would appear only when \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]\) is plotted instead; for second order it would be \(1/[\mathrm{R}]\) that plotted straight.

rows.stem: The treatment of ethyl bromide with alcoholic silver nitrite gives :
rows.solution:
Nitrite is an AMBIDENT nucleophile, and which atom attacks depends on how the reagent holds it. Silver nitrite is largely covalent, so the oxygen is tied up in the bond to silver and only the NITROGEN lone pair is free; attack through nitrogen gives the nitroalkane:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{AgNO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5NO_2} + \mathrm{AgBr}\)
The product is nitroethane. Potassium nitrite, being ionic, frees the whole ion and attack goes through oxygen instead, giving the isomeric ethyl nitrite — which is the distractor.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Which of the following aqueous solutions will have the highest freezing point ?
rows.solution:
Depression of freezing point is a colligative property, \(\Delta T_f = i\,K_f\,m\). The HIGHEST freezing point belongs to the solution with the SMALLEST depression, that is the smallest number of particles. All four are 1.0 M, so the van't Hoff factor decides: glucose does not dissociate, \(i = 1\); potassium chloride gives two ions, \(i = 2\); sodium sulphate gives three, \(i = 3\); aluminium chloride gives four, \(i = 4\).

The 1.0 M glucose solution therefore has the fewest particles, the smallest depression, and the highest freezing point. Reading the question as asking for the LOWEST freezing point would give aluminium chloride, which is the trap.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Which of the following aldehydes will undergo Cannizzaro reaction ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - all four options are printed as DRAWN 2-D condensed structures, the branch methyls hanging below the chain on vertical bond strokes: (A) CH3-CH-CHO with CH3 under the middle carbon; (B) (CH3)3C CHO written inline; (C) CH3-CH2-CHO written inline; (D) CH3-CH-CH-CHO with a CH3 under each of the two middle carbons. I NAMED nothing and instead rendered each as its standard condensed formula, which is a lossless reading of the drawing and does NOT state the answer (the student still has to count alpha-hydrogens). Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
Cannizzaro's reaction is given only by an aldehyde with NO \(\alpha\) hydrogen — no hydrogen on the carbon next to the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group. Check each:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CHO}\) has one \(\alpha\) hydrogen; \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}\) has two; \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH(CH_3)-CHO}\) has one.
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-CHO}\), 2,2-dimethylpropanal, has a fully substituted \(\alpha\) carbon and therefore NO \(\alpha\) hydrogen at all — so it is the one that undergoes Cannizzaro's reaction. The others, having \(\alpha\) hydrogens, undergo aldol condensation instead.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
In which of the following groups are both ions coloured in aqueous solution ?
I. \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\)    II. \(\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}\)    III. \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}}\)    IV. \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\)
[Atomic number : Cu = 29, Ti = 22, Co = 27, Fe = 26]
rows.solution:
Colour requires a partly filled d subshell, so work out each ion:
\(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\) — completely filled, COLOURLESS.
\(\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}\) is \(3d^{0}\) — completely empty, COLOURLESS.
\(\mathrm{Co^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{7}\) — partly filled, coloured.
\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{6}\) — partly filled, coloured.
So the pair in which BOTH ions are coloured is III and IV.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}\) can be distinguished by :
rows.solution:
Add sodium hydrogen carbonate solution. The carboxylic acid is strong enough to liberate carbon dioxide from it and gives a brisk effervescence; the aldehyde is not acidic and gives no reaction.
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH} + \mathrm{NaHCO_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2COONa} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}\)
Hinsberg's test is for amines and Lucas's for alcohols, so neither applies. The iodoform test would fail to distinguish them, since neither compound carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO-}\) group.

rows.stem:
Match the type of cell given in Column I with their use given in Column II.

| Column I | Column II |
|---|---|
| i. Lead storage cell | a. Wall clock |
| ii. Mercury cell | b. Apollo Space Programme |
| iii. Dry cell | c. Wrist watch |
| iv. Fuel cell | d. Inverter |
rows.solution:
Match each cell to the use its properties fit.
A lead storage cell is rechargeable and delivers a large current, so it suits an INVERTER — i-d.
A mercury cell is tiny and holds a constant \(1.35\) V for its whole life, so it suits a WRIST WATCH — ii-c.
A dry cell is cheap and disposable and its voltage may drift, so it suits a WALL CLOCK — iii-a.
A hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell is efficient and produces drinkable water, which is why it powered the APOLLO SPACE PROGRAMME — iv-b.
The matching is i-d, ii-c, iii-a, iv-b.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: While doing qualitative analysis in chemistry lab, Abhishek added yellow coloured potassium chromate solution into a test tube. He was surprised to see the colour of the solution changing immediately to orange. He realised that the test tube was not clean and contained a few drops of some liquid. Which of the following substances will be the most likely liquid to be present in the test tube before adding potassium chromate solution ?
rows.solution:
The colour change from yellow to orange is chromate turning into dichromate, and that happens on ACIDIFICATION:
\(2\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
So the test tube must have held an acid, and of the four liquids offered only hydrochloric acid is one. Sodium hydroxide and sodium hydrogen carbonate are both basic and would push the equilibrium the other way, keeping the solution yellow; methyl orange is an indicator, not a source of protons.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : For measuring resistance of an ionic solution an AC source is used.
Reason (R) : Concentration of ionic solution will change if DC source is used.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: An alternating source IS used for measuring the resistance of an ionic solution, so the Assertion is true. And the Reason gives the cause: a direct current would electrolyse the solution, discharging ions at the electrodes so that the composition changes while the measurement is being made, and depositing products that polarise the electrodes. Alternating current reverses many times a second, so no net electrolysis occurs and nothing accumulates. The Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Henry's law constant \((\mathrm{K_H})\) decreases with increase in temperature.
Reason (R) : As the temperature increases, solubility of gases in liquids decreases.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Henry's constant INCREASES with temperature, not decreases, so the Assertion is false. That follows from the law itself: \(x = p/K_H\), so a larger \(K_H\) means less gas dissolved.

The Reason is true — the solubility of gases in liquids does fall as the temperature rises, which is why warm water holds less dissolved oxygen and why a warm fizzy drink loses its gas faster. And it is exactly that falling solubility which makes \(K_H\) rise. So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true.

rows.subtopic: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The solubility of aldehydes and ketones in water decreases with increase in size of the alkyl group.
Reason (R) : Aldehydes and ketones have dipole-dipole interaction.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true. Solubility of aldehydes and ketones in water does fall as the alkyl group grows, and they do have dipole-dipole interactions.

But they answer different questions. What makes the smaller members soluble is HYDROGEN BONDING between the carbonyl oxygen and water; what reduces the solubility as the alkyl group grows is the increasing hydrocarbon bulk, which cannot hydrogen bond at all. Dipole-dipole interaction between the carbonyl molecules THEMSELVES is a separate matter, and it explains their boiling points rather than their solubility. So both are true and the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The boiling points of alkyl halides decrease in the order \(\mathrm{RI} > \mathrm{RBr} > \mathrm{RCl} > \mathrm{RF}\).
Reason (R) : The van der Waals forces of attraction decrease in the order \(\mathrm{RI} > \mathrm{RBr} > \mathrm{RCl} > \mathrm{RF}\).
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the second explains the first. Boiling point is set by the strength of the intermolecular forces, which here are van der Waals attractions; those grow with the size and polarisability of the halogen atom, so they run \(\mathrm{RI} > \mathrm{RBr} > \mathrm{RCl} > \mathrm{RF}\) — and the boiling points follow in exactly the same order. The Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Note the order is NOT set by bond polarity, which runs the other way: \(\mathrm{C-F}\) is the most polar bond and the fluoride the lowest boiling.

rows.stem: Calculate the elevation of boiling point of a solution when 3 g of \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) (Molar mass = 111 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) was dissolved in 260 g of water, assuming that \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) undergoes complete dissociation. (\(\mathrm{K_b}\) for water = \(0{\cdot}52\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
Calcium chloride dissociates completely into one \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) and two \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), so three particles per formula unit and \(i = 3\).

\(\Delta T_b = i\,K_b \times \dfrac{w_2}{M_2} \times \dfrac{1000}{w_1}\)
\(= \dfrac{3 \times 0.52 \times 3 \times 1000}{111 \times 260}\)
\(= 0.162\ \mathrm{K}\)

The factor of 3 is what the phrase "complete dissociation" supplies; without it the answer would be one third as large.

rows.stem: Liquids 'X' and 'Y' form an ideal solution. The vapour pressure of pure 'X' and pure 'Y' are 120 mm Hg and 160 mm Hg respectively. Calculate the vapour pressure of the solution containing equal moles of 'X' and 'Y'.
rows.solution:
The solution is IDEAL, so it obeys Raoult's law over the whole range and the total vapour pressure is the sum of the two partial pressures:
\(p_{\text{total}} = p_X^{\circ}x_X + p_Y^{\circ}x_Y\)

Equal moles of the two liquids means equal mole fractions:
\(x_X = x_Y = 0.5\)

Substituting,
\(p_{\text{total}} = 120 \times 0.5 + 160 \times 0.5 = 60 + 80\)
\(p_{\text{total}} = 140\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

Being ideal is what allows the straight arithmetic mean here; a non-ideal mixture would lie above or below 140 depending on the direction of the deviation.

rows.stem:
| Concentration of KCl solution in mol / L | Conductivity at \(298{\cdot}15\) K in S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) | Molar Conductivity at \(298{\cdot}15\) K in S \(\mathrm{cm^{2}\,mol^{-1}}\) |
|---|---|---|
| \(1{\cdot}000\) | \(0{\cdot}1113\) | \(111{\cdot}3\) |
| \(0{\cdot}100\) | \(0{\cdot}0129\) | \(129{\cdot}0\) |
| \(0{\cdot}010\) | \(0{\cdot}00141\) | \(141{\cdot}0\) |

Based on the data given above, give plausible reason for the variation of conductivity and molar conductivity with concentration.
rows.solution:
The two quantities move in OPPOSITE directions on dilution, and the table shows both.

CONDUCTIVITY DECREASES as the concentration falls — from 0.1113 to 0.00141 S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) here. Conductivity is the conductance of a UNIT VOLUME of solution, so it depends on how many ions that volume contains. Diluting spreads the same ions through a larger volume, so any given volume holds fewer current-carrying ions and conducts less.

MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY INCREASES as the concentration falls — from 111.3 to 141.0 S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\). Molar conductivity is the conductance of the volume containing ONE MOLE of electrolyte, so the number of ions is fixed by definition and only their mobility can change. On dilution the ions are further apart, interionic attraction falls, and they move more freely — so the same mole of electrolyte conducts better.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
(a) Write the rate law expression for the reaction \(2\mathrm{HI} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{I_2}\), if the order of the reaction is zero.
(b) What is the effect of temperature on the rate of reaction ? Write a mathematical expression for the same.
rows.solution:
(a) For a zero order reaction the rate does not depend on the concentration at all:
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{HI}]^0 = k\)
The decomposition of hydrogen iodide on a gold surface is the standard example, the surface being saturated so that adding more HI changes nothing.

(b) The rate INCREASES with temperature — roughly doubling for every \(10\ \mathrm{K}\) rise near room temperature. Raising the temperature greatly increases the fraction of molecules carrying energy equal to or above the activation energy. The mathematical expression is the Arrhenius equation:
\(k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}\)
or in logarithmic form \(\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}\).

rows.stem: Explain the mechanism of acid catalysed hydration of ethene.
rows.solution:
Acid catalysed hydration of ethene adds water across the double bond in three steps.

Step 1 — protonation of the alkene. The \(\pi\) electrons attack a proton from the hydronium ion, giving a carbocation:
\(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H_3O^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3-\overset{+}{C}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 2 — nucleophilic attack of water on the carbocation. A water molecule donates a lone pair to the positively charged carbon, giving a protonated alcohol, an oxonium ion:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-\overset{+}{C}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)

Step 3 — deprotonation. Another water molecule removes the extra proton, giving the alcohol and regenerating the hydronium ion:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_3O^+}\)

The catalyst is returned unchanged in the last step, which is what makes it a catalyst.

rows.stem:
(a) How can acetaldehyde be prepared from acetyl chloride ?
(b) Propanal is more reactive than propanone towards nucleophilic addition reaction. Give reason.
rows.solution:
(a) By Rosenmund's reduction. Acetyl chloride is hydrogenated over palladium supported on barium sulphate — a catalyst deliberately poisoned so that the reduction stops at the aldehyde instead of going on to the alcohol:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd\text{-}BaSO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

(b) Two reasons, both working the same way. Propanal has ONE alkyl group on its carbonyl carbon and propanone has TWO. Each alkyl group releases electron density towards that carbon by the inductive effect, reducing the partial positive charge the nucleophile is attracted to; and each also physically obstructs the nucleophile's approach. With one group instead of two, propanal's carbonyl carbon is both more electrophilic and less hindered, so it is the more reactive towards nucleophilic addition.

rows.stem:
Shweta mixed two liquids A and B of 10 mL each. After mixing, the volume of the solution was found to be \(20{\cdot}2\) mL.
(i) Why was there a volume change after mixing the liquids ?
(ii) Will there be an increase or decrease of temperature after mixing ?
(iii) Give one example for this type of solution.
rows.solution:
(i) Because the attraction between the unlike molecules is WEAKER than between the like ones. The volume after mixing, 20.2 mL, is greater than the 20 mL of the components, so the molecules are further apart than they were: the A-B interactions do not hold them as tightly as the A-A and B-B interactions they replaced. This is positive deviation from Raoult's law.

(ii) The temperature will DECREASE. Weaker new interactions mean energy has to be absorbed to separate the original molecules and is not fully repaid on mixing, so the process is endothermic and the mixture cools.

(iii) Ethanol and acetone. Ethanol and water, or carbon disulphide and acetone, are equally good examples of positive deviation.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
(i) How does sprinkling of salt help in clearing the snow covered roads in hilly areas ?
(ii) What happens when red blood cells are kept in \(0{\cdot}5\%\) (mass/vol) NaCl solution ? Justify your answer.
(iii) Write an application of reverse osmosis.
rows.solution:
(i) Salt dissolves in the thin film of liquid water always present on the snow, and a solution freezes below \(0\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). The ice is then above its own freezing point and melts; more salt dissolves in the melt and the process continues, so the snow turns to a solution that runs off and the road clears. The colligative property involved is DEPRESSION OF FREEZING POINT.

(ii) The red blood cells SWELL UP, and may burst. Human red cells have an internal concentration equivalent to about 0.9% sodium chloride, so a 0.5% solution is HYPOTONIC — more dilute than the cell contents. Water therefore flows INTO the cells by endosmosis, and if enough enters the cells rupture, a process called haemolysis.

(iii) Desalination of sea water. Applying to the sea water a pressure greater than its osmotic pressure drives the solvent backwards through a semi-permeable membrane, so fresh water is collected and the salts are left behind.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
For the reaction \(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightarrow\) Products, the following initial rates were obtained at various initial concentrations of reactants :

| Sl. No. | \(\mathrm{[A]/mol\ L^{-1}}\) | \(\mathrm{[B]/mol\ L^{-1}}\) | Initial rate \(\mathrm{/mol\ L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(0{\cdot}1\) | \(0{\cdot}1\) | \(0{\cdot}05\) |
| 2 | \(0{\cdot}2\) | \(0{\cdot}1\) | \(0{\cdot}10\) |
| 3 | \(0{\cdot}1\) | \(0{\cdot}2\) | \(0{\cdot}05\) |

Determine the order of the reaction with respect to A and B and overall order of the reaction.
rows.solution:
Compare the experiments in pairs, changing one concentration at a time.

Experiments 1 and 2: \([\mathrm{B}]\) is unchanged while \([\mathrm{A}]\) doubles from 0.1 to 0.2, and the rate doubles from 0.05 to 0.10. A doubling of concentration doubling the rate means the order with respect to A is 1.

Experiments 1 and 3: \([\mathrm{A}]\) is unchanged while \([\mathrm{B}]\) doubles from 0.1 to 0.2, and the rate does NOT change — it stays at 0.05. A concentration that can be doubled without affecting the rate enters to the power zero, so the order with respect to B is 0.

Order with respect to A: 1
Order with respect to B: 0
Overall order: \(1 + 0 = 1\)
Rate law: \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^1[\mathrm{B}]^0 = k[\mathrm{A}]\)

rows.stem:
(a) What is meant by crystal field splitting energy ? For a \(\mathrm{d^4}\) ion, write the configuration if (i) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} < \mathrm{P}\), and (ii) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} > \mathrm{P}\).
(b) Explain why in tetrahedral coordination entities, low spin configurations are rarely observed.
rows.solution:
(a) Crystal field splitting energy is the difference in energy between the two sets of d orbitals — \(t_{2g}\) and \(e_g\) in an octahedral field — produced when the ligands, treated as point charges, approach the metal in a definite geometry. Before they arrive the five d orbitals are degenerate; the ligands raise the energy of those pointing towards them more than the others, and the gap that opens is \(\Delta_0\).

For a \(d^4\) ion:
(i) When \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\) the field is weak, so promoting an electron costs less than pairing: \(t_{2g}^3\ e_g^1\), the high spin arrangement with four unpaired electrons.
(ii) When \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\) the field is strong, so pairing is the cheaper option: \(t_{2g}^4\ e_g^0\), the low spin arrangement with two unpaired electrons.

(b) Because in a tetrahedral field the splitting is too small. Only four ligands approach the metal, and none of them head-on along an orbital axis, so \(\Delta_t\) works out at about four-ninths of \(\Delta_0\) for the same ligands. It is therefore almost always LESS than the pairing energy, the electrons spread out rather than pair, and the complex is high spin. Low spin tetrahedral entities are correspondingly rare.

rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(a) The \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond length in chlorobenzene is shorter than that in methyl chloride.
(b) Grignard reagents should be prepared under anhydrous conditions.
(c) In case of optically active alkyl halides, \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reactions are accompanied by racemisation.
rows.solution:
(a) Because of resonance. In chlorobenzene the lone pair on chlorine is delocalised into the ring, so the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond acquires partial double bond character and is correspondingly shorter. The carbon is also \(sp^2\) hybridised rather than \(sp^3\), and an \(sp^2\) orbital has more s character and is smaller, which shortens the bond further. In methyl chloride neither effect operates: the carbon is \(sp^3\) and there is no ring to delocalise into.

(b) Because a Grignard reagent is destroyed by water. Its carbon-magnesium bond is strongly polarised with the carbon negative, so the reagent is a powerful base as well as a nucleophile, and even a trace of moisture protonates it to the alkane:
\(\mathrm{R-MgX} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-H} + \mathrm{Mg(OH)X}\)
The reagent must therefore be prepared and used in dry ether under anhydrous conditions.

(c) Because the \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) route passes through a PLANAR carbocation. The positively charged carbon is \(sp^2\) hybridised with its three bonds in one plane, so the nucleophile can approach with equal ease from either face. The two approaches give the two opposite configurations in equal amounts, and the product is a racemic mixture — optically inactive even though the starting material was not.

rows.stem:
(a) Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their acidic strength :
3,5-dinitrophenol, 4-methylphenol, phenol, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol
(b) What happens when : (write equations)
(i) Phenol is distilled with Zn dust ?
(ii) Anisole is treated with HBr ?
rows.solution:
(a) Acidity depends on how stable the phenoxide ion is once the proton has gone. An electron-RELEASING group destabilises it and weakens the acid; an electron-WITHDRAWING group stabilises it and strengthens the acid, and the more such groups the stronger the effect. The methyl group of 4-methylphenol releases electron density, so it is the weakest; phenol has no substituent; 3,5-dinitrophenol has two nitro groups; and 2,4,6-trinitrophenol has three. The increasing order of acid strength is
4-methylphenol \(<\) phenol \(<\) 3,5-dinitrophenol \(<\) 2,4,6-trinitrophenol

(b)(i) Distilling phenol with zinc dust reduces it, the zinc taking the oxygen away as zinc oxide and leaving the bare ring:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{Zn} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{ZnO}\)

(ii) Hydrogen bromide cleaves the ether, and the bond that breaks is the \(\mathrm{O-CH_3}\) one — the \(\mathrm{O-C_6H_5}\) bond has partial double bond character from resonance and is too strong. So the phenyl group keeps the oxygen:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OCH_3} + \mathrm{HBr} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3Br}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: An organic compound 'A' (molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_8H_8O}\)) gives 2,4-DNP test. It does not give Tollen's test, but gives a yellow precipitate 'B' with NaOH and \(\mathrm{I_2}\). On drastic oxidation, it gives a carboxylic acid 'C' with formula \(\mathrm{C_7H_6O_2}\). Identify 'A', 'B', 'C' and write the reactions involved.
rows.solution:
Every clue narrows the compound down. A positive 2,4-DNP test means a carbonyl group. Failing Tollens' test makes it a KETONE rather than an aldehyde. A yellow precipitate with sodium hydroxide and iodine is the iodoform reaction, so the carbonyl carries a METHYL group. And drastic oxidation to \(\mathrm{C_7H_6O_2}\), benzoic acid, shows a benzene ring with the side chain burnt back to a single carboxyl carbon. With the formula \(\mathrm{C_8H_8O}\) all of that fixes the compound as phenyl methyl ketone.

\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}\), acetophenone
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CHI_3}\), iodoform
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\), benzoic acid

The reactions:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} + \mathrm{H_2N-NH-C_6H_3(NO_2)_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5C(CH_3){=}N-NH-C_6H_3(NO_2)_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} + 3\mathrm{I_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CHI_3} + \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa} + 3\mathrm{NaI} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KMnO_4}/\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

rows.stem:
(a) Name the type of linkage responsible for the formation of proteins from \(\alpha\)-amino acids.
(b) Write any two differences between DNA and RNA.
rows.solution:
(a) The PEPTIDE linkage — the amide bond \(-\mathrm{CONH}-\) formed when the \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) group of one \(\alpha\)-amino acid condenses with the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group of the next and a molecule of water is lost.

(b) Two differences:
DNA is DOUBLE stranded, two chains coiled into a helix and held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, whereas RNA is normally SINGLE stranded.
DNA's sugar is 2-deoxyribose and RNA's is ribose; correspondingly DNA carries THYMINE where RNA carries URACIL. DNA also replicates itself, which RNA does not.

rows.stem: Give chemical reactions to show the presence of an aldehydic group and straight chain in glucose.
rows.context: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones that represent enormous structural diversity in terms of the arrangement of atoms in space, resulting in hundreds of stereoisomers. Although the chemical properties of most stereoisomers may not be very different, their metabolic rate and utilization in biological systems is significantly different and known to influence the overall carbohydrate metabolism. Structural variants, which arise due to a different arrangement of atoms in three-dimensional space are known as stereoisomers. The number of stereoisomers can be theoretically estimated by using the formula 2n, where 'n' is the number of stereocenters or asymmetric (chiral) carbon atoms in a molecule. Out of these stereoisomers, there are some structures, which are mirror images of each other, and they are referred to as enantiomers.
rows.solution:
The ALDEHYDIC group. Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent that attacks an aldehyde and nothing else, and it converts glucose to the six-carbon monocarboxylic gluconic acid:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2\ water}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
A ketonic carbonyl would not be oxidised under these conditions, so the carbonyl in glucose must be an aldehyde.

The STRAIGHT CHAIN. Heated for a long time with hydriodic acid, glucose is reduced completely — every oxygen stripped away — and what remains is \(n\)-hexane:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HI},\ \Delta} \mathrm{CH_3(CH_2)_4CH_3}\)
Since the carbon skeleton cannot rearrange under these conditions, the six carbons must already have been in an unbranched chain.

rows.stem: Define anomers.
rows.context: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones that represent enormous structural diversity in terms of the arrangement of atoms in space, resulting in hundreds of stereoisomers. Although the chemical properties of most stereoisomers may not be very different, their metabolic rate and utilization in biological systems is significantly different and known to influence the overall carbohydrate metabolism. Structural variants, which arise due to a different arrangement of atoms in three-dimensional space are known as stereoisomers. The number of stereoisomers can be theoretically estimated by using the formula 2n, where 'n' is the number of stereocenters or asymmetric (chiral) carbon atoms in a molecule. Out of these stereoisomers, there are some structures, which are mirror images of each other, and they are referred to as enantiomers.
rows.solution: Anomers are a pair of stereoisomers of a monosaccharide that differ in configuration at ONE carbon only — the anomeric carbon, which is C-1 in an aldose and C-2 in a ketose. That carbon becomes a new stereocentre when the open chain closes into its cyclic hemiacetal form. \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and \(\beta\)-D-glucose are the standard pair, differing only in whether the C-1 hydroxyl points below or above the ring.

rows.stem: Draw the structure of \(\beta\)-D-Glucopyranose.
rows.context: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones that represent enormous structural diversity in terms of the arrangement of atoms in space, resulting in hundreds of stereoisomers. Although the chemical properties of most stereoisomers may not be very different, their metabolic rate and utilization in biological systems is significantly different and known to influence the overall carbohydrate metabolism. Structural variants, which arise due to a different arrangement of atoms in three-dimensional space are known as stereoisomers. The number of stereoisomers can be theoretically estimated by using the formula 2n, where 'n' is the number of stereocenters or asymmetric (chiral) carbon atoms in a molecule. Out of these stereoisomers, there are some structures, which are mirror images of each other, and they are referred to as enantiomers.
rows.solution:
\(\beta\)-D-Glucopyranose is the six-membered ring form, drawn as a Haworth projection: a flat hexagon with the ring oxygen at the back right and the carbons numbered clockwise from the anomeric carbon, C-1, at the right.

Going round the ring: C-1 carries \(-\mathrm{OH}\) pointing UP and \(-\mathrm{H}\) down; C-2 carries \(-\mathrm{OH}\) down and \(-\mathrm{H}\) up; C-3 carries \(-\mathrm{OH}\) up and \(-\mathrm{H}\) down; C-4 carries \(-\mathrm{OH}\) down and \(-\mathrm{H}\) up; C-5 carries \(-\mathrm{H}\) down and the \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) group, which is C-6, pointing UP; and the ring oxygen bridges C-5 to C-1.

What makes it the \(\beta\) anomer is the C-1 hydroxyl pointing UP, on the SAME side as the \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) group. In the \(\alpha\) anomer that one hydroxyl points down instead, and nothing else changes.

rows.stem: Sucrose is known as invert sugar. Explain.
rows.context: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones that represent enormous structural diversity in terms of the arrangement of atoms in space, resulting in hundreds of stereoisomers. Although the chemical properties of most stereoisomers may not be very different, their metabolic rate and utilization in biological systems is significantly different and known to influence the overall carbohydrate metabolism. Structural variants, which arise due to a different arrangement of atoms in three-dimensional space are known as stereoisomers. The number of stereoisomers can be theoretically estimated by using the formula 2n, where 'n' is the number of stereocenters or asymmetric (chiral) carbon atoms in a molecule. Out of these stereoisomers, there are some structures, which are mirror images of each other, and they are referred to as enantiomers.
rows.solution:
Strictly it is the HYDROLYSIS PRODUCT of sucrose that is called invert sugar, and the name records a change of sign in the optical rotation.

Sucrose itself is dextrorotatory. Hydrolysis gives an equimolar mixture of glucose, which is dextrorotatory, and fructose, which is laevorotatory — and fructose rotates so much more strongly that it outweighs the glucose. The net rotation of the mixture is therefore to the LEFT, the opposite of what the sucrose gave, so the rotation has been inverted during the hydrolysis and the product is called invert sugar.

rows.stem: One mole of \(\mathrm{CrCl_3 \cdot 4H_2O}\) precipitates one mole of AgCl when treated with excess of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution. Write (i) the structural formula of the complex, and (ii) the secondary valency of Cr.
rows.context: Werner's coordination theory in 1893 was the first attempt to explain the bonding in coordination complexes. It must be remembered that this theory was put forward before the electron had been discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897, and before the electronic theory of valency. Werner did not have any of the modern instrumental techniques and all his studies were made using simple experimental techniques. Werner was able to explain the nature of bonding in complexes and he concluded that in complexes, the metal shows two different sorts of valency : primary and secondary. Primary valences are normally ionisable whereas secondary valences are non ionisable.
rows.solution:
(i) One mole of silver chloride precipitated per mole of compound means only ONE chloride is free in solution, so the other two must be inside the coordination sphere. With six positions to fill and two taken by chlorides, the four water molecules complete the sphere:
\(\mathrm{[Cr(H_2O)_4Cl_2]Cl}\)

(ii) The secondary valency is the coordination number, the count of ligand donor atoms bonded directly to the metal — four aqua ligands and two chlorido ligands, so 6.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: What is the difference between a complex and a double salt ?
rows.context: Werner's coordination theory in 1893 was the first attempt to explain the bonding in coordination complexes. It must be remembered that this theory was put forward before the electron had been discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897, and before the electronic theory of valency. Werner did not have any of the modern instrumental techniques and all his studies were made using simple experimental techniques. Werner was able to explain the nature of bonding in complexes and he concluded that in complexes, the metal shows two different sorts of valency : primary and secondary. Primary valences are normally ionisable whereas secondary valences are non ionisable.
rows.solution:
A DOUBLE SALT is an addition compound of two simple salts which exists only in the solid state: dissolve it in water and it dissociates COMPLETELY into its simple ions, so nothing of its identity survives in solution. Mohr's salt, \(\mathrm{FeSO_4 \cdot (NH_4)_2SO_4 \cdot 6H_2O}\), gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{NH_4^+}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\).

A COMPLEX keeps its coordination sphere intact in solution: the ligands stay bound to the metal and it is the complex ion that goes into solution. \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\) gives \(\mathrm{K^+}\) and \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\) but no free cyanide — which is why it is not poisonous although potassium cyanide is.

rows.stem:
Arrange the following complexes in the increasing order of conductivity of their solution :
\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_3Cl_3]}\), \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\), \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2}\)
rows.context: Werner's coordination theory in 1893 was the first attempt to explain the bonding in coordination complexes. It must be remembered that this theory was put forward before the electron had been discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897, and before the electronic theory of valency. Werner did not have any of the modern instrumental techniques and all his studies were made using simple experimental techniques. Werner was able to explain the nature of bonding in complexes and he concluded that in complexes, the metal shows two different sorts of valency : primary and secondary. Primary valences are normally ionisable whereas secondary valences are non ionisable.
rows.solution:
Conductivity depends on the NUMBER OF IONS the compound gives in solution, so count the ions released by each.

\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_3Cl_3]}\) has all three chlorides inside the sphere, so it is neutral and gives NO ions — lowest conductivity.
\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2}\) has two chlorides outside, so it gives THREE ions: one complex cation and two chlorides.
\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\) has all three chlorides outside, so it gives FOUR ions — highest conductivity.

Increasing order of conductivity:
\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_3Cl_3]} < \mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2} < \mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\)

rows.stem: Write two differences between primary and secondary valences in coordination compounds.
rows.context: Werner's coordination theory in 1893 was the first attempt to explain the bonding in coordination complexes. It must be remembered that this theory was put forward before the electron had been discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897, and before the electronic theory of valency. Werner did not have any of the modern instrumental techniques and all his studies were made using simple experimental techniques. Werner was able to explain the nature of bonding in complexes and he concluded that in complexes, the metal shows two different sorts of valency : primary and secondary. Primary valences are normally ionisable whereas secondary valences are non ionisable.
rows.solution:
Two differences:
The PRIMARY valency is IONISABLE — the ions satisfying it are released in solution and can be precipitated — whereas the SECONDARY valency is NON-IONISABLE, the ligands satisfying it staying bound to the metal.
The primary valency is satisfied by NEGATIVE IONS only, whereas the secondary valency is satisfied by negative ions OR neutral molecules.

The primary valency also corresponds to the oxidation state and is not directional, while the secondary valency is the coordination number and fixes the geometry of the complex.

rows.stem:
(i) For a galvanic cell, the following half reactions are given. Decide, which will remain as reduction reaction and which will be reversed to become an oxidation reaction. Give reason for your answer.
(I) \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cr\,(s)}\); \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}} = -\,0{\cdot}74\) V
(II) \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe\,(s)}\); \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}} = -\,0{\cdot}44\) V
(ii) Represent the cell in which the following reaction takes place :
\(\mathrm{Mg\,(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\,(0{\cdot}001\ \mathrm{M}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\,(0{\cdot}100\ \mathrm{M}) + 2\mathrm{Ag\,(s)}\)
Calculate \(\mathrm{E_{cell}}\) if \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{cell}} = 3{\cdot}17\) V. (log 10 = 1)
rows.solution:
(i) Reaction (II) will REMAIN a reduction and reaction (I) will be REVERSED to become an oxidation.

In a galvanic cell the half reaction with the HIGHER reduction potential occurs as written, at the cathode, and the other is reversed at the anode. Here \(E^{\circ} = -0.44\) V for iron is higher than \(-0.74\) V for chromium, so iron is reduced and chromium oxidised — that is, chromium's low reduction potential makes it the better reducing agent, and it gives up electrons to the iron. The cell reaction is
\(2\mathrm{Cr(s)} + 3\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{Fe(s)}\)
with \(E^{\circ}_{cell} = (-0.44) - (-0.74) = +0.30\) V, positive as a spontaneous cell requires.

(ii) The anode is written on the left and the cathode on the right, each with its concentration:
\(\mathrm{Mg(s)} \mid \mathrm{Mg^{2+}}(aq,\ 0.100\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{Ag^+}(aq,\ 0.001\ \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{Ag(s)}\)

Two electrons are transferred, so \(n = 2\):
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Ag^+}]^2}\)
\(= 3.17 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{0.100}{(0.001)^2} = 3.17 - 0.0295\log 10^{5}\)
\(= 3.17 - 0.0295 \times 5 = 3.17 - 0.1475\)
\(= 3.0225\ \mathrm{V}\), about \(3.02\ \mathrm{V}\)

rows.stem:
(i) State Kohlrausch's law. Give any two applications of it.
(ii) \(\Lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mathrm{NH_4Cl}\), \(\Lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mathrm{NaOH}\) and \(\Lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mathrm{NaCl}\) are \(129{\cdot}8\), \(217{\cdot}4\), and \(108{\cdot}9\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{2}\,mol^{-1}}\) respectively. Molar conductivity of \(1 \times 10^{-2}\) M solution of \(\mathrm{NH_4OH}\) is \(9{\cdot}33\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{2}\,mol^{-1}}\). Calculate the degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) of \(\mathrm{NH_4OH}\) solution at this concentration.
rows.solution:
(i) Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions states that at infinite dilution the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the individual limiting contributions of its cation and its anion, each counted as many times as the formula unit provides it.

Two applications:
It gives the limiting molar conductivity of a WEAK electrolyte, which cannot be obtained by extrapolating a conductivity curve because that curve has no straight portion near the origin.
It allows the degree of dissociation, and hence the dissociation constant, of a weak electrolyte to be calculated from \(\alpha = \Lambda_m/\Lambda^{\circ}_m\).

(ii) Build the limiting value for ammonium hydroxide from three strong electrolytes. The first two supply \(\mathrm{NH_4^+} + \mathrm{Cl^-}\) and \(\mathrm{Na^+} + \mathrm{OH^-}\), and subtracting the third removes the \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), leaving exactly \(\mathrm{NH_4^+} + \mathrm{OH^-}\):
\(\Lambda^{\circ}_m(\mathrm{NH_4OH}) = \Lambda^{\circ}_m(\mathrm{NH_4Cl}) + \Lambda^{\circ}_m(\mathrm{NaOH}) - \Lambda^{\circ}_m(\mathrm{NaCl})\)
\(= 129.8 + 217.4 - 108.9 = 238.3\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The degree of dissociation is then
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda^{\circ}_m} = \dfrac{9.33}{238.3} = 0.039\), that is \(3.9\%\)

rows.stem:
(i) In a chemistry practical class, the teacher gave his students an amine 'X' having molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_7N}\), and asked the students to identify the type of amine. One of the students, Neeta, observed that it reacts with \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\), to give a compound which dissolves in NaOH solution. Can you help Neeta to identify the compound 'X' ?
(ii) Arrange the following in the increasing order of their \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) value in aqueous phase :
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}\), \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\)
(iii) Aniline on nitration gives considerable amount of meta product along with ortho and para products. Why ?
(iv) Convert aniline to :
(I) p-bromoaniline
(II) phenol
rows.solution:
(i) Hinsberg's reagent, benzenesulphonyl chloride, gives with a PRIMARY amine a sulphonamide that still carries a hydrogen on nitrogen; that hydrogen is acidic, so the product dissolves in sodium hydroxide. A secondary amine leaves no hydrogen on nitrogen and gives an alkali-insoluble product, and a tertiary amine does not react at all. Neeta's compound therefore dissolved because 'X' is a PRIMARY amine, and the only primary amine of formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_7N}\) is
\(\mathrm{X} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\), ethanamine (ethylamine)

(ii) A lower \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a stronger base, so increasing \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) lists the STRONGEST base first. For methyl groups in water the three effects — inductive, steric and solvation — settle with the secondary amine strongest, then the primary, then the tertiary; ammonia, with no alkyl group at all, comes next; and aniline, whose lone pair is delocalised into the ring, is by far the weakest. Increasing \(\mathrm{pK_b}\):
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{NH} < \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} < (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{N} < \mathrm{NH_3} < \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)

(iii) Because nitration is carried out in a strongly ACIDIC medium, and there aniline is largely protonated to the anilinium ion. The \(-\mathrm{\overset{+}{N}H_3}\) group is deactivating and META directing, whereas the free amine is activating and ortho, para directing. The two pathways run side by side, so a substantial meta product appears alongside the ortho and para ones — about 47% meta in practice.

(iv)(I) Aniline to p-bromoaniline. Acetylate first to moderate the activating power of the nitrogen, brominate, then hydrolyse the protecting group off:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{pyridine}]{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NHCOCH_3} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_3COOH}]{\mathrm{Br_2}} \mathrm{4\text{-}Br{-}C_6H_4{-}NHCOCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{OH^-}\text{ or }\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{4\text{-}Br{-}C_6H_4{-}NH_2}\)
Without the acetylation bromine water would put three bromines on at once.

(II) Aniline to phenol. Diazotise and then warm the aqueous solution, so that water replaces the diazonium group:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{NaNO_2} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow{0-5\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow[283\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5OH}\)

rows.stem:
(i) Arun heated a mixture of ethylamine and \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\) with ethanolic KOH, which forms a foul smelling gas. Write the chemical equation involved.
(ii) Identify A and B in the following reactions :
\(\mathrm{A} \xrightarrow[\text{ethanol}]{\mathrm{H_2/Pd}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xleftarrow{\mathrm{Br_2/NaOH}} \mathrm{B}\)
(iii) Convert aniline to :
(I) benzene
(II) sulphanilic acid
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - sub-part (ii) is printed as a two-dimensional reaction scheme in which the CENTRAL compound is DRAWN (a Kekule benzene hexagon bearing \(\mathrm{NH_2}\) at its top vertex) rather than named, with 'A' to its left under a right-pointing arrow labelled \(\mathrm{H_2/Pd}\) above and 'ethanol' below, and 'B' to its right under a LEFT-pointing arrow labelled \(\mathrm{Br_2/NaOH}\). I NAMED it losslessly as \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\) (aniline), which does not state the answer - the question asks for A and B, and aniline is the given. The row is therefore answerable from its text. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(i) This is the carbylamine reaction, and the foul-smelling gas is the isocyanide. A primary amine warmed with chloroform and ethanolic potassium hydroxide gives it:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH\ (EtOH)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_2H_5NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)
The test responds only to primary amines, which is what makes the smell diagnostic.

(ii) Both arrows lead TO aniline, so each starting material must be a compound aniline can be made from by that reagent.
Hydrogen over palladium in ethanol REDUCES a nitro group, so
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2}\), nitrobenzene
Bromine in sodium hydroxide is the Hofmann bromamide degradation, which gives an amine with ONE CARBON FEWER than the amide, so the amide must have seven carbons:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2}\), benzamide

(iii)(I) Aniline to benzene. Diazotise, then reduce the diazonium group away with hypophosphorous acid or ethanol:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{NaNO_2} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow{0-5\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}} \mathrm{C_6H_6}\)

(II) Aniline to sulphanilic acid. Concentrated sulphuric acid first protonates the nitrogen to give anilinium hydrogensulphate; heating to \(453-473\ \mathrm{K}\) rearranges it, and the sulphonic acid group ends up PARA to the amino group:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}H_3\,HSO_4^-} \xrightarrow{453-473\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{4\text{-}H_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}SO_3H}\)

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
(i) When pyrolusite ore is fused with KOH, in presence of air, a dark green coloured product 'A' is obtained which changes to purple coloured compound 'B' in acidic medium.
(I) Write the formulae of 'A' and 'B'.
(II) Write the ionic equation for the reaction when compound 'B' reacts with \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) in acidic medium.
(ii) Give reasons :
(I) \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) in aqueous solution is a good oxidising agent.
(II) The actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction.
(III) \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Zn^{2+}/Zn}}\) value is more negative than expected, whereas \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Cu^{2+}/Cu}}\) is positive.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) Pyrolusite is manganese dioxide. Fusing it with potassium hydroxide in air oxidises manganese from \(+4\) to \(+6\), giving the dark GREEN manganate; acidifying that makes it disproportionate, and the PURPLE permanganate appears.
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\), potassium manganate
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{KMnO_4}\), potassium permanganate

(II) Acidified permanganate oxidises iron(II) to iron(III) and is itself reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\):
\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\)

(ii)(I) Because \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) reverts to \(\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}\), which is the common and stable oxidation state of the whole lanthanoid series. Being reduced is therefore strongly favoured, and a species readily reduced is by definition a good oxidising agent.

(II) Because the 5f orbitals of the actinoids are more diffuse and shield the nuclear charge even less effectively than the 4f orbitals of the lanthanoids. The effective nuclear charge felt by the outer shells therefore rises faster from one actinoid to the next, and the contraction per element is greater.

(III) Both are explained by the special stability of the ion formed or not formed. \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\), a completely filled subshell of unusual stability, so zinc gives up its two electrons readily and its potential is more negative than the trend predicts. Copper is the opposite case: its high enthalpy of atomisation and high ionisation enthalpies are not repaid by the hydration enthalpy of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), so forming the hydrated ion is unfavourable overall and \(E^{\circ}\) comes out positive — the only positive value in the series.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) While studying the periodic properties, Arti came across an abnormal behaviour in the atomic size of Hf. She found that, even though Hf is placed below Zr in the same group, both have almost similar atomic sizes.
(I) Which phenomenon is responsible for the above behaviour ? Define it.
(II) Mention any other consequence of the above phenomenon.
(ii) Give reasons for the following :
(I) Transition metals exhibit catalytic properties.
(II) Transition metals have high enthalpy of atomisation.
(III) Sc is a transition element, while Zn is not.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) LANTHANOID CONTRACTION is responsible. It is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series from lanthanum to lutetium, caused by the poor shielding that 4f electrons give: as each is added the effective nuclear charge felt by the outer shells grows and pulls them in. By the time the series is passed, the cumulative shrinkage cancels the increase that the extra period would otherwise give, so hafnium ends up almost the same size as zirconium above it.

(II) Another consequence: the lanthanoids themselves become progressively harder to separate from one another, because their ionic radii shrink so gradually that their chemical properties are nearly identical. The basic character of their hydroxides also decreases steadily from \(\mathrm{La(OH)_3}\) to \(\mathrm{Lu(OH)_3}\), as the shrinking ion holds the hydroxide more tightly.

(ii)(I) Because they show VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES, so they can accept electrons from one reactant and pass them to another, offering a lower-energy path and returning to their original state at the end. Their partly filled d orbitals also let reactant molecules adsorb on the metal surface and form intermediates there, and a finely divided metal offers a large surface area.

(II) Because both the \((n-1)d\) and the \(ns\) electrons take part in the metallic bonding. With a large number of unpaired electrons available for interatomic bonds, the metallic bonding is strong and a great deal of energy is needed to break the lattice into free atoms.

(III) Because scandium has an INCOMPLETELY filled d orbital and zinc does not. Scandium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^1 4s^2\), so its d subshell is partly filled in the ground state. Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^2\), and its only common ion \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\) — completely filled both in the ground state and in its oxidised state — so it fails the definition of a transition element.
